title: Corey Ruiz's family should guide police legislation, Stubbs says - The Cap Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. More than a month after Madison police shot and killed 38-year-old Corey Ruiz, Democratic state Rep. Shelia Stubbs said she is following his family’s lead on any legislative actions she could take in the next session in response to the shooting. Ruiz, a Black man from Madison, was shot and killed by Officer Kiel Baitinger-Peterson on July 22 at the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin streets. Officers chased Ruiz, who was on a bicycle, after being called to the neighborhood for a person who was checking parked cars. They eventually intercepted Ruiz at the east side intersection where a physical struggle took place in the street. Officials say Ruiz pulled out a knife and injured Baitinger-Peterson, who then shot Ruiz after two other officers deployed a Taser “without success.” Stubbs quickly stood by Ruiz’s family’s side in support and was among the first lawmakers to speak out on the incident. She represents parts of Madison, Monona and McFarland in the state Assembly. She has served in the Assembly since 2019 and is up for reelection in November, running against Republican Henry Johnson, a student at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. During her time as a lawmaker, Stubbs has been a leading advocate for racial equity and police reform, and she’s been in office during several incidents of violent police encounters with Black men, including the 2015 shooting death of Tony Robinson Jr. in Madison, the 2020 death of George Floyd in Minneapolis and the 2020 shooting of Jacob Blake in Kenosha. Everett Mitchell, a Dane County Circuit Court judge and senior pastor of Christ the Solid Rock Church, adds votives to the base of the Vel Phillips statue during a demostration for Corey Ruiz, held by the African American Council of Churches at the Wisconsin Capitol. If she is reelected to a fifth term, Stubbs said she has ideas on legislation she could propose next session stemming from Ruiz’s death, such as changes to state laws relating to body-worn cameras, mental health, fleeing and eluding, and oversight committees. She also criticized the city of Madison for not having body cameras and not participating in a 2022 grant program to help police departments buy the video equipment. But ultimately, she said, it is up to Ruiz’s family members and their attorney, well-known civil rights lawyer Ben Crump, to shape any specific changes they want in state law. “It’s whatever they want,” Stubbs told the Cap Times. “I will be introducing whatever it is that they ask of me.” In 2020, Republican Assembly Speaker Robin Vos appointed Stubbs to co-chair a legislative task force on racial disparities, which Vos created in response to the global outrage that followed Floyd’s death. The task force introduced a package of 18 bills that included reforms such as requiring crisis intervention training and drug testing of police officers. Nine of the task force’s bills were enacted into law, including a new statewide standard for law enforcement use of force, a restriction on choke holds and new requirements for police agencies to track data on incidents such as use of force and no-knock search warrants. Rep. Shelia Stubbs previously co-chaired a legislative task force on racial disparities following the 2020 death of George Floyd. “It was a start,” Stubbs said of the task force’s accomplishments. “By all means it wasn’t meant to be the final bills. I think you learn from every incident.” In addition to Stubbs and other legislators, the 32-person task force included pastors, police, protesters, nonprofit leaders, educators and a diverse group of community members. It was important to bring many different voices and stakeholders to the table, Stubbs said. Stubbs said others told her it was “political suicide” to serve on the task force, but she felt it was important for her to be part of the conversation because of her own experiences as a Black woman. “What I did know is I believed in change, and what I did know is I couldn’t sit around and just not do something, right? And that’s where I’m at with the Ruiz family. I want to do what it takes for outcomes. We couldn’t save Corey,” Stubbs said. “But we can save the next person, because we have an opportunity. And I think what people have to do is take accountability.” One of the task force bills from 2021 that did become law established a one-year grant program for Wisconsin police agencies to buy body-worn cameras. In total, 48 agencies across the state were awarded grants from the program in 2023, totaling more than $1.2 million, according to data provided by the Wisconsin Department of Justice. Some Madison-area agencies applied for and received a grant, including the city of Middleton, the village of Belleville and Iowa County. The Madison Police Department, the only law enforcement agency in Dane County that does not widely use body cameras, did not apply for this state grant. Stubbs called it “unacceptable” that the city’s police officers did not have body-worn cameras at the time of Ruiz’s death. “We created the state funding opportunity,” Stubbs said of the grant program. “Madison Police Department has to own up to it that they didn’t seize the opportunity.” She added: “When people say, ‘What is the state doing?’ We did something. What did the municipality do? They failed to apply.” City officials have debated the body cameras' use for years, with worries over costs and potential misuse of footage. In 2024, the city participated in a pilot program, equipping 41 police officers with body cameras for 90 days. Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said she plans to include funding for body-worn cameras in the next budget, and the city plans to apply for a federal grant to help with the purchase of the equipment. But long-term costs to operate a body-worn camera program present a challenge for the city, the mayor said, and state revenue restrictions on municipalities add to that hurdle. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway speaks at a press conference after an encampment at the memorial for Corey Ruiz was cleared by the city. “Trained staff will be needed to manage and maintain the equipment, as well as preserve, catalog and store the video footage so it’s available to the public. Those costs must come out of the city’s operating budget. Local governments in Wisconsin are severely restricted financially by the state. Rising costs make it a challenge just to continue the services we are already providing to Madison residents,” Rhodes-Conway said. “The lack of options provided by the state makes adding anything new to our operating budget — particularly staff — very difficult.” Stubbs said the state’s grant program was successful and that she is willing to look at other legislation around body cameras such as another grant or a requirement that local governments buy and use them. But again, she said, she wants Ruiz’s family to decide. Ruiz’s death opened old wounds for Stubbs, who said the shooting harkened back to other trauma her community has felt, like the deaths of Robinson and Floyd, and the Abundant Life Christian School shooting in 2024, which happened in her district. Stubbs recalled protesting and marching late into the evening after Floyd’s death. “During that time it was just really traumatic. It was draining. It was emotional,” Stubbs said. “I’m not afraid to share I cried a lot.” But she said she is taking lessons from the past as the community navigates what’s next after Ruiz’s death. She learned through those experiences and on the task force that leaders need to listen to the community. The Cap Times welcomes tips from readers to help us inform our community. Email tips@captimes.com or visit captimes.com/tips for more options. “That’s what I think people look for at a moment like this, that you at least show up. When you are elected, you got to show up to work,” she said. “You gotta face the heat.” She said she also remains focused on writing policy that will become law. For years, Republicans have controlled the state Legislature and the proposals that move in and out of both chambers. But Democrats have had their eyes set on winning a trifecta this fall — controlling the Assembly, the Senate and the governorship — which Stubbs said will “absolutely” make it easier for reforms to be implemented. “I look forward to being in the majority, and I look forward to getting work done across this state that has just been on a hiatus,” Stubbs said.

raw.summary: Corey Ruiz's family should guide police legislation, Stubbs says  The Cap Times

summary: Following a fatal police shooting, state lawmaker Shelia Stubbs criticized Madison for failing to apply for state body-camera grants. Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway defended the city, pointing to financial constraints, state revenue restrictions, and ongoing plans to fund body cameras in the upcoming budget.
